The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Wise (for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources) that Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Oil Substitution and Conservation Act and the Canadian Home Insulation Program Act, be now read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works; and the amendment of Mr. Hockin (p. 3227).

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying this morning, when I started speaking to the Bill before the House, ever since the present Govenment came to power, the only Bills we have had to discuss have been Bills that were bad for this country, and that is unfortunate. I think it is important to recall, for the benefit of all the Conservative Members here in the House who have probably neither read the Bill nor realize what is being cut, that the Canadian Oil Substitution Program represents $95 million that this Government has cut. This program was helping consumers to convert their heating systems to electricity, natural gas or other forms of renewable energy.
There is $85 million in the Canadian Home Insulation Program. This program provided for taxable grants of up to a
March 26, 1985

maximum of $500 for home insulation. Now these grants are going to be cut from 60 per cent to 3316 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, this Government cannot find the money to meet the needs of Canadians but it can find the money to send 1,000 more members of our Canadian Forces to Europe at a cost of $100 million per year. They have no trouble finding money there.
Mr. Speaker, instead of getting involved in star wars, this Government should have gotten involved in the war against unemployment. If it refuses to withdraw this Bill, it should at least extend the program for six months so that everyone who applied after the Minister's announcement that he would make cuts in his program, will still have a chance to benefit from those grants.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from a letter sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) by the President of the Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers Association of Canada:

Aware of your interest in Quebec problems-
He did not know what was coming when he wrote that.
-we take the liberty of making a request concerning the Canada Oil Substitution Program (COSP).
As you undoubtedly know, COSP has been very popular in Quebec. As a result of its termination slated for March 31, 1985, there has been an unprecedented increase in the number of orders from manufacturers of equipment needed to convert to electric heating. We have received so many orders that we fear they may not be filled without compromising equipment safety and quality.
We therefore urge you to extend the deadline, at least with respect to the installation of new equipment. Applications might be submitted until March 31 and the equipment installed between now and August 31, 1985. Such an extension would not require additional expenditures.
Well, Mr. Speaker, these are experts and specialists in energy conversion who are urging the Government to extend the program for at least six months so as to enable Canadians to apply and make sure that conversions meet all safety standards.
Mr. Speaker, I said earlier that the Government cannot find any money to help needy Canadians and has to cut their benefits. However, when a banking institution is about to go belly up, it has no trouble finding millions of dollars. When it comes to increasing the salary of its friends, its former candidates, as my colleague pointed out with respect to Mr. Hanni-gan, then money is the last of its concerns.
Mr. Speaker, not only did the Government drop the insulation program, it also shirked its responsibilities concerning the removal of UFFI, another cut-back of $1.5 million. Many Canadians were counting on grants of up to $5,000 to renovate and remove UFFI products from walls in their homes.
There again the Government did not bother to consult anybody before imposing cut-backs on all Canadians, as it did in the case of unemployment insurance, housing and insulation. No consultation with the people. But when it comes to showing off, our Prime Minister has proved that as a master of
Oil Substitution Act
ceremonies, he is second to none, presiding over major conferences where spokesmen for industry, unions and consumers represent their fellow Canadian citizens.
And then, at a cost of $1 million a day, they decided to have a huge consultation, but everybody knew full well that the federal government had already made up its mind, contrary to the promise that party had made during the election and the day following its victory, and contrary to the statement the Prime Minister himself had made, as reported in today's Citizens: "You're going to see tens upon tens of jobs being created just as quickly as a new government can be sworn in." Since September 4, because of its stupid decision to try and bring down the deficit on the backs of workers and middle and low-income Canadians, what the government has created is not new jobs, but increased unemployment.
I know that most of my colleagues, that members from both the NDP and the Liberal Party are firmly against this bill. I know also that the greater majority of my colleagues of the Progressive Conservative Party are privately against this bill too, but that they lack the necessary fortitude to stand up and say so publicly. They prefer to hide, play the ostrich and bury their heads in the sand, Mr. Speaker.
You are signaling that my time is about to expire, Mr. Speaker, but I hope a number of Tory members will finally wake up, remember that they were elected to protect the interests on their respective constituents, and not to spin yarns on behalf of their leader.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by saying that I always try to take Governments and Opposition Parties at their word. So far we have had about 17 hours or five sitting days to debate this Bill at second reading. All Parties in the House agreed on the original legislation. Therefore, I do not think it was remiss on the part of Members on all sides of the House to use a few days debating a major change in the legislation which the entire House supported unanimously in 1981.
As an ordinary country boy from the Prairies, I had assumed that even the Conservatives knew that you could not lay a gas pipeline on the Prairies in February or March. They not only want to shut off the debate, they want to shut off 150 homes on Rural Route 2 northwest of Regina. I admit that I have some interest in that area. Under the present Conservative Government of Saskatchewan, the Saskatchewan Power Corporation had devised a good policy to take natural gas to more villages, hamlets and individual farms in the Province of Saskatchewan. These people and the Saskatchewan Power Corporation have been planning to instal a number of new lines based on their number of potential users. They used this Bill as the premise to make a survey of potential customers. Now that the program is to be cancelled, people are not finding the immediate cost effectiveness that there was before. Saskatchewan Power is putting in a new line on Rural Route 2 outside of Regina. It is slated for completion in June. There

March 26, 1985
Oil Substitution Act
are 150 people along that line who have signed up for the service. I suspect that Sask Power operates similarly to power corporations in other provinces which require a sign-up of 65 per cent before they proceed to build a gas pipeline or power line. In this case there is a 100 per cent sign-up. I presume the Tories must have been in Florida all winter if they believe that a plastic or steel pipeline can be installed in February or March.
I realize that a six-month hoist amendment is usually a parliamentary ploy under the rules to kill a Bill. However, this is a rare instance when we moved a six-month hoist in order to delay the passage of this Bill so that the ground could thaw and people who signed up for grants could benefit. That was the simple reason for our proposal.
My hon. friends across the way should recognize that the ground is still frozen and if they want this legislation to pass now I invite them to dig the trenches and install the gas pipelines for 150 homes, mostly farm homes, northwest of my city.
Surely the Government must recognize the sense of encouraging people to convert to less costly fuel services. In 1981 the COSP legislation, which was retroactive to 1980, received second reading in one hour in the House. That means there was unanimous consent by all Parties. This legislation was to have effect until 1990. All the power corporations in every province, every municipal utility corporation and tens of thousands of Canadians based their plans on that assumption. It is not right to change the rules in the middle of the game.
If the Government wishes to change the policy under this legislation it has every right to do so, but there should be reasonable notice given before it proceeds. While our Party has recommended a six-month hoist, I believe this legislation should be delayed for at least one year to account for thousands of Canadians who wanted to convert to natural gas. Some of these Canadians have had to convert to propane temporarily until natural gas pipelines are installed. They are now faced with the problem of the lack of propane tanks.
The effect of this legislation will be the exact opposite to the Government's intention to increase the number of jobs. The COSP Program provided more jobs than will be created if it is ceased. We made a simple proposition but the Conservatives believe that a plastic or steel pipeline can be laid before the end of March, which is only a few days from now. The ground in Toronto may still be frozen even by the end of April. However, it seems that the Conservatives do not understand that logic.
We should support any program that will reduce the requirement for imported oil, that saves Canadian foreign exchange, creates more jobs and gives the Government a return on its investment. I remind Hon. Members that this program is an investment, not an expense. I hope that my hon. friend, the Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), would agree that this is an investment whose returns will outnumber the cost to the taxpayers.
It is obvious that a reduction in the requirement for imported oil in Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic Provinces will provide extra jobs and increase the use of Canadian resources, particularly natural gas.
In conclusion, let me quote the Hon. Member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) who has been a respected Member of the House from western Canada for almost 30 years. As a major spokesman for the Conservative Party in the debate in 1981, when the Conservatives joined with the Liberals and NDP in supporting this legislation that was to be effective until 1990, he said, as reported at page 11099 of Hansard for June 30, 1981:
I do not think there is any question that the House in general understands and supports the purpose of the oil substitution program-
Is the Government trying to help Imperial Oil sell more oil or is it trying to help individual Canadians reduce their heating costs? Let me quote further from Hansard of June 30, 1981. The Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain said:
It is a good philosophy to get as many people in the low technology systems as possible to move away from the consumption of oil. It is particularly good, if the alternative is cheaper not only than the present price of oil but the future price as well.
The Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain concluded by congratulating the Government and the Minister, on behalf of the Conservative Party, for bringing in this legislation. He said, as reported at page 11101 of Hansard:
1 hope he will consider the suggestion that I have made to improve the legislation and make it available to all Canadians. If so, we could achieve this conversion from oil to other energies more rapidly than this bill can by itself.
I ask my hon. friends opposite to reconsider what they are doing. I ask them to maintain the commitments made in 1981. I ask them to permit this Bill to be extended and I hope they will persuade the Minister to do so, so that tens of thousands of Canadians, provincial power corporations and municipal utilities can live up to the contracts they have signed.
I cannot understand why the Government is reversing its position after those people have acted in good faith. I hope that Members of the Government will persuade the Minister to reconsider this legislation. If so, they will get full support and approbation from both Opposition Parties.

Mr. Speaker, the decision of the Government to repeal the Oil Substitution and Conservation Act and the Canadian Home Insulation Program Act is another indication of its insensitivity, in that these programs helped many average and low-income Canadians. The people who will lose the benefits of these programs are out there today watching the actions of the Government and wondering what they elected on September 4. While these programs are going down the drain, what happens? The office of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is given a 57 per cent increase in its budget, and its staff is increased by 30. Also the public relations budget of the Government has been increased by 10 per cent. That money
March 26, 1985

will be used to advertise its conferences, seminars and other meetings rather than to do things for Canadians.
We have heard much in the House about the consultative process. I wonder how many average and low-income Canadians were consulted about the cutting of these program. They have heard much about expensive conferences, but they have not heard too much in support of their efforts to conserve energy. The Upper Ottawa Valley of eastern Ontario has some of the highest levels of unemployment since the Diefenbaker Government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: That is a great endorsation of the Grits.

The highest levels of unemployment, I say to the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid). The Grits brought in programs which were useful to the people of that area and in turn to their communities. Coming from a highly populated area of this province, the Hon. Member would not be as sensitive to that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Oh.

What he is doing right now clearly demonstrates the insensitive character of the Government.
The UIC regulations are another example of this insensitivity. It will now take into consideration every penny a person earns over a period of time in order to cut back in UIC payments. In many small communities where employment was scarce, people made use of COSP and CHIP. They switched from oil to another form of energy. Any benefit they received for changing from oil to another form of energy automatically increased their disposable income. In the Town of Deep River, three years ago, one home out of three was heated with electricity. I would expect that the number is even higher today as a result of COSP over the last few years. Undoubtedly more people went off oil. Canadians in small communities and in rural areas are conservation-minded. They are the ones who repair their windows.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext: And their doors.

That is correct, they fix their doors. They repair their basements and their foundations. They improve the insulation in their homes. In some cases even the small contractors that benefited from CHIP complained that the program was inadequate. I hope the Government realizes that by cancelling these programs it is actually taking away business from small business at a time when it is bragging in the House that it is in favour of small business. Also it is taking away the jobs of Canadians who work in those industries.
In recent years there has been much research into solar energy and the use of wood to heat homes. It is part of the off-oil system.
Oh?

The Hon. Member does not seem to be well informed. I am glad that I am speaking about it; perhaps he will gain some knowledge. In recent years new stoves have
Oil Substitution Act
been designed to use wood in the heating of homes. This is related to the off-oil program. Many other new technologies have been adopted. For example, waste is being used in burners to heat sawmills which produce the waste in the first place. This provides great efficiency. That program was sponsored by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. It assisted small businesses, sawmills and planing mills to change from oil to a system capable of burning waste products to heat their premises. Also attention has been paid to considerable heat loss problems.
Along with all these benefits, these programs have made people more aware of the necessity to conserve energy. The system by which farm homes are heated today has changed dramatically. If any part of the industrial society requires all the assistance it can get, certainly it is the agricultural industry. Many people do not look upon agriculture as an industry, but indeed it is an industry, one of our largest. We should do everything we can to assist it in saving money by changing over to cheaper methods of operation. That is certainly in our interest. It all comes down to the industrial plants which produce the products used in the off-oil program and those which produce the insulation and other materials used to improve home heating systems. Surely that great old slogan that we heard so much about-jobs, jobs, jobs-is the very thing that comes to mind. By the repealing of this legislation, the Government is taking away jobs from people. That is another form of insensitivity.
We have heard a lot about consensus building. What kind of consensus building was done when the decision was made to remove this program? I wonder if at the same time that this Government is planning to remove this program which benefits the average and small-income people, it is thinking of greater technology and the production of other jobs in that area. There is the projected Slowpoke III reactor that uses 5 per cent enriched uranium and produces heat very cheaply, there is a prototype of the slowpoke IV reactor being made at this very moment at Whiteshell, Manitoba, with 5 per cent enriched uranium. It produces both heat and energy. These are some of the things we will have to look at in the future.
A lot of research has been done on waste connected with the operations of nuclear energy. Canada should continue that route of putting emphasis on nuclear energy in this country, the production of heat for homes and municipalities at a cheap rate and with even greater benefit than has been produced in the hydroelectric field by the Candu reactor.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about Bill C-24. This legislation is very important for Canadians. The debate in the House today is on whether or not we are prepared to maintain these two government programs and thus create many jobs here in Canada.

March 26, 1985
Oil Substitution Act

For some reason the Government seems to have forgotten about ordinary Canadians. For some reason it has decided to eliminate the Canadian Home Insulation Program, to get rid of that program and the off-oil program. Both these programs would help a lot of ordinary people. They would create jobs for those who put in the insulation, convert the furnaces, dig the trenches for gas lines and other jobs of that sort.
I want to say in particular a few words with regard to Saskatchewan. I see the Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Scowen) and one or two Albertans in the House, although Bow River is in southern Alberta. The ground is frozen in Saskatchewan until at least March 31. This point was made by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). It is very difficult to put in a gas line in frozen prairie ground.
Use dynamite.

My Tory friend from Quebec says they should use dynamite. I would like to see him come to Kam-sack, Saskatchewan to put in a gas line and convert a furnace from oil to gas. The former Prime Minister would not agree with that. That shows the insensitivity of this Government. I know that the Member who was formerly Prime Minister of this country would agree that it shows the insensitivity of the federal Government to the special problems of northern Canada and the Prairies that it would end the off-oil program and the Canadian Home Insulation Program while the ground is still frozen on the Prairies. There is no understanding of the reality of that situation in central and northern Saskatchewan. Therefore, I appeal to the Government to extend this program for another year, or certainly extend it for another three, four, five or six months so that it will be fair to all Canadians. Why are some Canadians more special than others?
The Government says that through this program it will save approximately $350 million a year. This very same Government is going to give corporate welfare to the oil companies this year to the tune of some $1.7 billion. It is a continuation of the old Liberal policy called PIP. It is good enough for the rich, but there is no money for ordinary Canadians. The former Prime Minister must be very embarrassed about this Bill in Parliament today. He is fidgeting in his seat. 1 know he would love to get up and speak against this Bill.
I also know that he has a lot of respect for this institution of Parliament. If he were Prime Minister, he would not bring in a Bill of closure that affects ordinary Canadians. Today we are dealing with closure. I remember speech after speech of Conservative Members in the last Parliament when going after Liberals, saying they had no respect for Parliament, that they were bringing in closure on matters that affected ordinary people. This Government is doing exactly the same thing that it whined, cried and complained about when in opposition. That is a bit of hypocrisy that I did not expect to see when we had a change of government in this country.
The other important issue is the whole question of the creation of jobs. During the campaign, we heard speech after speech by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) saying that the
most important issue is jobs, jobs, jobs. I would like to see some Conservative back-benchers get up and tell me why it would eliminate this program, which would create thousands and thousands of jobs for people who need them because they are unemployed, and at the same time spend $1.7 billion under the PIP program to assist the big oil companies in this country. Over five years, it will cost $8.6 billion of taxpayers' money. I know the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) must be very upset and frustrated by this continuation of Liberal policy. I know that he will be supporting us in this debate. I know that he will get up and speak on behalf of ordinary Albertans. It must make him as angry as it makes me to see this program for insulating houses and saving oil being discontinued.
By the way, we would save about 75,000 barrels of oil a day, a lot of it Albertan oil, if the programs were continued. Instead, this Government is going to cut them off and spend the money helping wealthy Canadians, the big oil companies. Yesterday the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDou-gall) said we would spend millions of dollars of taxpayers' money to help salvage a big bank in Canada, the Canadian Commercial Bank. We are making interest-free loans. There is all kinds of taxpayers' money being used to prop up this bank. Who are the depositors? The Canadian chartered banks and the foreign banks have $150 million on deposit. The trust companies have money on deposit. Greymac had money on deposit. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few words to what has already been said. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) and the Government of Canada have decided to cut off the Canadian Oil Substitution Program which was established some four years ago. In addition, the Government has decided to terminate, ahead of schedule, the Canadian Home Insulation Program. The Government has said that these programs are being terminated to save money. According to certain Conservative Members, the most needy have already been taken care of and only the fairly well-off have not yet taken advantage of the program. However, as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has stated, the main intent of the Bill is to save money for the Government of Canada. As previous speakers have pointed out, it does not make sense when compared with other initiatives which the Government has taken.
I would like to make reference to a point which was made by a member of the NDP with respect to PIP. He asked why so much money-indeed, billions of dollars-was being spent to pay oil companies for the cost of drilling. The amounts are absolutely staggering. They run into billions of dollars. The answer to the Hon. Member's question is quite simple. The answer lies in the reason PIP was introduced in the first place and why the Government cannot simply discontinue the Petroleum Incentives Program. If the Government did that, the oil companies would not drill for oil in the offshore areas. There would be no activity off the coasts of Newfoundland or Nova Scotia if the Petroleum Incentives Program were not in place. It is interesting to note the amounts of money which are involved and the fact that the money goes directly to the oil companies from the federal Treasury after the drilling is finished.
The Government of Canada is in a difficult position. During the election campaign it said that it would do away with PIP and replace it with a tax incentive program at the end of the year. However, we have not heard anything about that. In fact, the Estimates still show the same amount of money for the oil companies which are exploring. Let there be no doubt that once that money is removed, a lot of oil companies which are presently drilling for oil off the east coast of Canada will also be removed. I suppose it is only fair to make reference to that, since we are debating COSP.
Many people imagine Newfoundland as being a rich territory, like the Clampett's on television used to live in where there was black gold and Texas tea and everybody became millionaires because of oil. The fact is that the only thing which most Newfoundlanders know about oil and gas is that the prices have increased drastically. The prices have increased for two main reasons. Of course, one of those reasons is the taxes which have been placed on the bottom line by the provincial Government of Newfoundland. When people have to pay 22 per cent on the bottom line to fill up their cars on top of the increased charges-because Newfoundlanders are at the end
Oil Substitution Act
of the line as far as the distribution system for gasoline and oil is concerned-then we can see why this program is so important.
It is important that some financial assistance be given to the people who want to convert and get away from burning oil in their furnaces and stoves. It should always be kept in mind that without the incentive which that program provides, a great many families will not be able to convert to wood.
There has been a lot of discussion in the House about the conversion to other sources of energy, but not very much of that discussion has concerned wood. If we examine the figures that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources presented to the House, we see why wood conversion is so important to provinces such as Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. When we look at the projections of the Department, we find that some 59 per cent of the residences it thought would qualify and convert to wood have not to date converted. When we look at the yearly figures we discover that the projections of the Department have shown far fewer people than the numbers which actually utilized the program. There has been 126 per cent achievement over what it projected would take place during the years this program has been in effect. So we are left with 59 per cent of the total number of dwellings which were thought would convert over a ten-year period. We are still left with that 59 per cent in Newfoundland which have not converted mainly to wood.
We also have to keep in mind that this Bill today does away as well with the possibility of having more hospitals in the Province of Newfoundland convert to wood chips. This was something which happened over the last few years because of this legislation and the incentives which were provided.
I think the bottom line is that we have in this chamber today a Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who brings in legislation to remove money from the hands of ordinary Canadians and poor people who need that little grant to install a wood stove in the basement in order to give that person some heat. Those people don't want to pay $500 a month for oil in the months of December, January, February and March. They want to be able to put a chunk of wood in their furnace in the evening when they go to bed, and that one chunk of wood in the type of stove now being used would last the entire night.
These poor people who are looking for a little bit of assistance, a measly $800 to convert to wood, are now having that opportunity taken away from them. They will now be left to the fortunes of whatever side of the bed the federal Government gets out of in the morning. That will determine what the price of oil is which these people will have to pay to operate their furnaces.
Before the election the Conservative Party said it was not going to increase oil and gas prices-just the opposite. We can talk all day about the PIP program and all of the philosophical arguments about the rich being the only ones left who did not take advantage of the program. We can talk about the fact that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in January

So Canadian oil is sold at a cheaper price to the United States than it is to Canada since the month of January. Here we have the bottom line, Mr. Speaker. We come from all that philosophy down to this Bill, and this Bill takes away a simple $800 from the pockets of a poor person in Canada who wants to convert to wood or to another energy source. That is the bottom line in this debate and that is what the bottom line should be. Let no other Hon. Member proclaim again that only the rich people are left, that all the poor people have taken advantage of the program. As I mentioned before to an Hon. Mr. Speaker, I am also very pleased to take part in this debate. May I say at the outset that I was extremely disappointed that the Government with its huge majority should choose to move closure, all the more so since this program has always been and still is quite popular in Quebec. In recent years, this program has gained wide support and acceptance among Canadians because they realized that it had two major objectives. The first major objective was to reduce demand in traditional energy sectors, in keeping with Canada's energy policy.
The second objective, aspect or benefit is that conversion in one case and insulation in the other led to a significant decrease in heating costs so that, as a direct consequence, hundreds of thousands of Canadians found it less expensive to keep their homes well heated. All of a sudden, practically overnight, they simply decide to cancel both programs. To me, this was a very harsh and totally unacceptable decision, so much so that for months now our offices have been swamped with hundreds of letters urging us to give consumers more time to benefit from this program which has proved to be extremely popular.
I can only say that the reaction of our constituents is quite understandable. Not so long ago I came across some statistics concerning the Maritime Provinces where the program gained such wide acceptance that nearly 80 per cent of eligible households applied under these programs. The situation in Quebec may not be as encouraging, but still 30 per cent of eligible applicants did benefit from the program.
I can appreciate the attitude of the Minister of State (Small Businesses) (Mr. Bissonnette) when he says that Quebecers
know one thing for sure-the Conservatives are not there to pamper Quebec, they are there to administer Canada.
Well, perhaps I might remind Government Members who gained the confidence of Canadians last September 4 that they may not be there to pamper Quebec, but that is no excuse to disregard basic principles of justice and fairness in the distribution of public funds.
I think we should also recall that before the election on September 4, the present Government had promised to create hundreds of thousands of jobs. They promised they would deal with the problem on a grand scale. They promised to deal with the problems of the agricultural sector. They promised to reduce interest rates. They promised to stabilize the dollar. They promised that more services would be available. It did not turn out that way, however. Not only have they failed to deal with any problem of substance, they have managed to create a host of new ones. Unemployment is as substantial as it was before September 4. Interest rates are rising. The dollar is losing ground every week. And now, in addition to all those problems, they are adding one more, which comes as a shock to Canadians who were counting on making certain changes in their homes in the next few months, in order to reduce their heating bills.
I think the use of closure is absolutely undemocratic. We must not forget that the Government has 211 Members. On the basis of this historic majority, the Government should give the opposition parties a chance to demonstrate the relevance of all the arguments in favour of this program and let them try to persuade the Government to act fairly and equitably towards all Canadians and especially those who, for various reasons, have not yet been able to proceed with conversion and take advantage of the grants available.
In concluding, I would urge those Members who are supposed to represent the interests of Quebec to consider the flagrant injustice of the fact that not quite 30 per cent of Quebec homeowners have been able to take advantage of this admirable program, while statistics for Western Canada show that 80 per cent were able to take advantage of the program in those provinces. Therefore, we must provide an extension. We must extend the deadline to provide a fair deal for these Canadians who, like many others have already done, would like to take advantage of a program that has proved its worth from every point of view.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak on Bill C-225, an Act to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act. This very important legislation has been introduced in this House on several occasions. The purpose of the Bill is straightforward and yet fundamental, and is set out in the Explanatory
March 26, 1985

Notes. It is to implement the repeated recommendation of the Canadian Human Rights Commission that "sexual orientation" be added as a prohibited ground of discrimination at the federal government level. At the present time under federal law, gays and lesbians receive no legislative protection from discrimination under federal jurisdiction.
The Bill would include as a prohibited ground of discrimination "sexual orientation" in addition to the other grounds which are set out in the Canadian Human Rights Act. As well, provisions of the legislation would require that the Canadian Human Rights Commission conduct a comprehensive study of all federal legislation and regulations to determine which, if any, might discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation and to report the results of that study to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) within one year of the coming into force of the Bill. Subsequent to that report, the Minister would be required to report back to the House on the steps that he has taken to remove the discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation from all existing federal legislation.
I might say initially that this occasion is, I suppose, somewhat historic in the following sense. This Bill or a similar Bill has been introduced in this House on a number of occasions. On each occasion on which it has been introduced, members of the Opposition or members of the Government have talked the Bill out. I am very pleased that the Government, through the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Speyer), has agreed that for the first time in the history of this nation this very important question will in fact be studied and given the thoughtful study that it deserves.
I understand that the Government is prepared to allow the subject matter of this Bill to be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. That committee has struck a special subcommittee which is charged with the very important responsibility of examining the implications of the coming into effect of Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
One of the issues which is being addressed by that subcommittee which I have the honour to be a member, is the whole question of the extent to which current federal legislation and practices may discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation. Therefore, I welcome the commitment of the Parliamentary Secretary as well as of the Chairperson of that subcommittee, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer), who has recognized the importance of study without in any way precluding a decision to be made by that committee.
The parliamentary subcommittee is considering the whole question of equality rights. As I have indicated, one of the questions that has been addressed by the Minister of Justice in that study is the question of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. I have noted as well that each year for the last four years the Canadian Human Rights Commission has strongly urged Parliament to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act as I have suggested in this Bill, that is, to include the provisions dealing with sexual orientation.
There are some who ask why it is necessary, why the Government should add sexual orientation as a prohibited
Canadian Human Rights Act
ground of discrimination and what is the need for change in this area of the law. After all, we are not dealing with a visible minority. Certainly there continues in Canada today to be a great deal of discrimination against visible minorities. The report Equality Now, an excellent report which was tabled in the last Parliament, has documented the extent of discrimination against visible minorities.
I would suggest that gays and lesbians in Canada today continue to be subject to discrimination and to many of the hardships and much of the pain that is faced by visible minorities. Indeed, I would venture to suggest that if all of the gays and lesbians in Canada were to suddenly become tomorrow a visible minority, Canadians would realize the extent to which gays and lesbians are active in our community, indeed are active in communities across Canada at all levels of our society.
There is still a great deal of discrimination. Gays and lesbians are still the victims of too much pain and too much violence in Canada. Discrimination exists in hiring practices at the federal level. One of the most glaring examples of that discrimination, of course, was the recent firing of five women from the Canadian Armed Forces, women with an outstanding record of service to the forces and to their country. They were treated as common criminals. They were interrogated by military police. They lost their jobs and lost their livelihood.
I would urge that this Parliament recognize that that is a grave injustice. Policies which allow for the Firing of gays and lesbians from the Armed Forces, policies which prevent the hiring on the basis of sexual orientation in the Armed Forces, RCMP or External Affairs, are policies which have no place in the law books of Canada today.
I would suggest as well that we must look seriously at federal statutes, including the Criminal Code, the Canada Labour Code, the Public Service Employment Act, the Income Tax Act and the Immigration Act. To the extent that this legislation discriminates on the basis of sexual orientation, that legislation too should be amended. In the case of the Criminal Code, for example, there are still far too many discriminatory provisions in the area of gross indecency which perpetrate an unequal age of consent, provisions with respect to bawdy-house laws which have been used in a repressive manner against the gay community and which, once again, should not be in the Criminal Code today.
I spoke earlier of pain and I spoke of violence. Once again, we do not have to deal just with the pain and the violence of the five women who were fired from their jobs in Nova Scotia. We are reminded of the tragic death, the suicide of a middle-aged married man in St. Catharines who burned himself to death after he was arrested on a gross indency charge. I would suggest that to the extent that this Parliament fails to act to put an end to discrimination against gays and lesbians, we must all share to a certain extent in the tragedy and in the responsibility for tragedy that occurs because such discrimination continues.
I recently met with a group of gays and lesbians in Sudbury in northern Ontario. One of the people who was there was a

March 26, 1985
Canadian Human Rights Act
young high school student. He spoke to me of the harassment, the taunts and, yes, the beatings that he faced in his school because of the fact that he happens to be gay. That cannot be acceptable in Canada today.
The National Gay Task Force of the United States documented in an excellent report on anti-gay and lesbian victimization the fact that violence continues to be far too widespread. The introduction to the report reads:
After centuries of oppression, invisibility, and isolation, gay and lesbian people have claimed the right to participate fully in society and to enjoy the same rights and privileges accorded heterosexuals. In the ensuing struggle, ever greater numbers have "come out" and built new relationships, institutions and communities.
While greater visibility has helped to strengthen gay/lesbian self-respect and community, for many it has resulted in greater vulnerability to violence and crime. Now that lesbians and gay men have a higher profile, they are more readily identifiable to those who deliberately seek to victimize them because of their sexual orientation.
The report goes on to document the very serious statistics indicating that more than nine in 10 of the respondents to the survey put out by the task force indicate that they experienced some form of victimization because of their sexual orientation. That can include threats of violence and being punched, hit, kicked or beaten.
As well, there is an added dimension of oppression and pain and that is the oppression of having to conceal one's sexual identity from one's friends, one's family and one's fellow employees. That particular form of oppression can be just as invidious. When the Canadian Coalition of Lesbians and Gay Men appeared before the Constitution Committee, this was put very eloquently in the following terms:
In the present circumstances, gay people are either vulnerable to discrimination, or are forced to try to escape such oppression by concealing their sexual identity. Neither alternative can be countenanced in a democratic society. The first alternative offends the principle of minority rights. The second alternative is surely one of the most oppressive forms of discrimination-to pressure people into lives built around deception and lies. Imagine what it would be like for heterosexuals to be either exposed to unjustified discrimination against them, or to be forced to conceal their husbands and wives from co-workers, to never be truthful about their home lives.
That is the situation today.
1 would like to make it very clear that this Bill is not in any way a statement of endorsement of a particular lifestyle. Once again, it is clear that the Bill is not suggesting that the majority does or does not endorse homosexuality as a way of life, but rather that we genuinely accept the principle of supporting the rights of a minority. It is one thing to recognize that someone has a right to do something, and something quite different to say that it is the right thing for that particular person to do.
The majority of Canadians recognize that democratic civil liberties require the elimination of discrimination against gays and lesbians. Just as the native Indian needs protection from racism and women need protection from sexism, gay people need protection in law from homophobia.
There are other forms of violence to which gay people are subjected. The violence of certain extreme elements of the Evangelical community like the Jimmy Swaggarts of the t.v. world incites people to violence under the guise of Christian philosophy. I suggest that this is a perversion of Christian philosophy. When people say things like Jimmy Swaggart did in his publication The Evangelist, we know that there are problems. After quoting from the Old Testament, he said:
In Old Testament days the practising homosexual was stoned to death.
He went on to quote from Romans and then said:
God is saying here that not only is the homosexual worthy of death, but (perhaps) also those who approve of homosexuality.
That kind of hate literature has no place in Canada today. Those same purveyors of hatred have promoted the hatred of gays and lesbians by taking advantage of public concern over the deadly disesse AIDS. There is in our community today a health care crisis. In the last three years in Canada, 105 people have died from AIDS and the incidence is increasing dramatically. It is therefore essential that we improve the level of funding of research as well as education about this deadly disease in a sensitive and responsible manner.
In conclusion, I would argue that the time has surely come for us in Canada to recognize that no man and no woman should be denied the fundamental equality of access to jobs, housing and services on the basis of his or her sexual orientation. Changes in the laws will not overnight change the hearts and the minds of people whose response to gays and lesbians promotes pain and oppression. However, such changes are an essential first step toward the creation of a society in which each individual is recognized for his or her inherent worth and dignity as a human being. Such changes in the law will hopefully also hasten the day when no man or woman and no young student in Sudbury or anywhere else in the country will be the victim of fear, violence and intolerance because he or she happens to be gay or lesbian. That day cannot come too soon.

speakeroldname: Mr. Chris Speyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some weeks ago, a parliamentary subcommittee was established for the purposes of studying in detail across the country the question of equality rights in Canada. The Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) has quite accurately stated that the subject matter of the Bill on which he spoke should properly go before that subcommittee.
I would like to emphasize that in no way does my Party associate itself with the comments made by the Hon. Member. Nevertheless, he is correct that the matter should be referred to the subcommittee because the subject matter ought to be studied and voted upon and a report ought to be made to the Justice Committee and in turn to the House.
I suspect that very soon in this debate there will be another motion which would refer the entire subject matter of the Bill to the subcommittee on justice. The Government accedes to that request because it has already had many other such requests and notices of testimony that will ensue with respect to that subject matter.
March 26, 1985

I do emphasize that the reflections and submissions that have been made today by the Hon. Member for Burnaby in no way reflect upon what I personally believe nor upon what Hon. Members on this side of the House believe.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak on this matter and to move a motion. I do not know whether or not a member of the Liberal Party wishes to speak. If not, I will speak briefly and move the motion to which the Parliamentary Secretary referred.
First, I would like to congratulate the Government for setting up the committee on equality and I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer) who is present. He is a new Member. I would like to point out that he had better be successful with this committee. I grew up in Etobicoke-Lakeshore. If the Hon. Member is not successful, I will come back and run against him. I am sure he will have some measure of success with this committee.
I was listening to the words of the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). He said that just as the native Indians need protection from racism and women need protection from sexism, gay people need protection in law from homophobia. In 1984, it still takes courage to say those kinds of things in the Canadian Parliament. People will read Hansard of today years in the future and will wonder why I am saying this. However, it is a fact of life that it is still very courageous for someone to take on those issues.
The riding of Vancouver-Kingsway was once represented by Angus Maclnnis. Against a tidal wave of public opinion, he took up the cause of the Japanese-Canadians from 1941 to 1945. Unfortunately, he is not here to see some of the results of his labours and realize that in 1985 something is being done to correct the wrong that was done to the Japanese-Canadians. We are now acknowledging the hurt and the consequences of the actions which the Government took back then. It took a long time for society to respond to that issue.
His wife, Grace Maclnnis, was the only female Member in the House of Commons in 1968. Today, there are many female Members in the House who are very active. When we see the swell and tide of the women's movement today we realize that sometimes it takes a long time to accomplish things.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby is courageous, outspoken and on the cutting edge of some of these issues. I applaud him, and apparently his electors do as well, as he received a handsome mandate in the last election.
The Hon. Member made reference to the gentleman who committed suicide after an unfortunate incident in southwestern Ontario. There could be a lot of debate about that issue, but I believe that all reasonable Canadians must feel that that suicide was a waste. Did that man have to do that? Are we in a society which forces a person to feel so much guilt that he has to commit suicide? He was a family man. There is something wrong. That suicide should not have happened. Therefore, I
Canadian Human Rights Act
look forward to hearing representations on these matters in committee.
The Parliamentary Secretary should not back off too quickly, because basically we are recognizing equality. I feel as a social democrat-and I think my feeling is shared by others- that we are discussing equality. I think we all agree that people should be treated equally, without discrimination. We should end discrimination wherever possible in Canada. I think we are all committed to that. It is one of the things which makes Canada such a great country.
I welcome the Bill and the fact that the Government has referred it to committee. In addition, I am glad that the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore is chairing the committee. I am sure he will do a good job as he is well qualified. Again, I salute the Hon. Member for Burnaby for his courage, tenacity and willingness to tackle these very important civil liberty issues in Canadian society. It is a tradition which was evident in the CCFf and is evident in the NDP and in other Parties. People such as Gordon Fairweather, John Diefenbaker and Pierre Trudeau also worked very hard on these important issues.
I would like to move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-225, and Act to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act, be not
now read a second time but that the Order be discharged, the Bill withdrawn
and the subject-matter thereof referred to the Standing Committee on Justice
and Legal Affairs".

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to make a few remarks on the Bill under consideration introduced by the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), not to mention the amendment moved by the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell).
First I want to congratulate both Members on their courage to raise in the House an issue which is highly controversial but which, in my opinion, in 1985, must be discussed in Parliament, be it here in the House or in one of the committees.
As Hon. Members know, illegality surrounding the whole question of homosexuality disappeared with the adoption of an omnibus Bill introduced by a Liberal Government in 1968. At the time, it was said that the Government did not have any business in the bedrooms of the nation. To put it shortly, the purpose of the 1968 Bill was to remove any suggestion of criminality from homosexual relationships. However, the mes-

March 26, 1985
Canadian Human Rights Act
sage conveyed to the Canadian public was not that this House, the then Government and the Opposition Parties wanted to encourage or promote homosexuality in Canada by adopting that Bill. On the contrary, the House was attempting to tell Canadians that they should show tolerance and acceptance of principles which are not necessarily endorsed by the majority. In a sense, it was a way of alleviating the tyranny of the majority over minorities, over people who oftentimes share marginal ideas.
The fact remains that there is a widely spread sentiment among Canadians today, including those who do not share the views of the gay community, that persons who belong to that minority group do suffer from discrimination, that time has come to debate the issue in the Canadian Parliament and to take appropriate measures so that protection under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms be readily available to all Canadians.
I think that the matter ought to be referred to committee. Indeed, I commend the Government for seeing it that way. Besides, I would suggest that the amendment moved by the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway makes it easier to debate the issue: we are not going to refer the Bill to committee, only the subject-matter of the Bill. The question is: Does the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms provide enough protection against discrimination with respect to homosexuals?
Mr. Speaker, we need only mention the provincial charters and especially that of my own province, Quebec, which contains provisions to protect people against discrimination on the basis of homosexuality. I think that unless we want to go through life with blinkers on, we can hardly object to the subject of the Bill being referred to an appropriate committee of the House for discussion. I realize that some Canadians may not agree with a proposal to add a provision protecting homosexuals. However, if the subject is referred to committee, they will have a chance to express their views, and it will also be an opportunity for those who favour this point of view to come here to Ottawa before Parliament to express their opinion.
Personally, I support the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway. I think the time has come to discuss this question openly here in Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak quite briefly and not in any way to challenge the intent of the amendment or the original indication of the Parliamentary Secretary that this matter be referred to committee. I would just like to go on record as expressing regret for part of the remarks of the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), namely, his reference to Evengelical Christians. I do not think those comments added to the merit of his address. In fact, they detracted from it, and I think that someone in this Chamber should make that point for the record.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that one does not increase understanding and tolerance for one group of Canadians by indicating intolerance and rejection for another group of Canadians. Let us try to maintain in as wide a frame of reference as possible this desire for understanding and try to get inside the point of view of those with whom we disagree. We should ask ourselves what they are trying to say and what they represent.
I certainly, as much as the Hon. Member for Burnaby, abhor any incitement to violence against any group of Canadians. However, I think we must respect the values and convictions which have been part of Canada and its traditions, traditions which Canadians must honour.
I welcome the decision of the Government's spokesman to refer this matter to committee for a number of reasons. First, I think we need to take a very searching look, as a Parliament, at this proposal. We cannot do that within the time available in this hour. We need the more thorough inspection which can be given by the committee. We need to hear from the various groups within Canada who will make representations to the committee, and we may, indeed, find that worth-while things are said against the proposal, things which this Parliament needs to hear and considerations this Parliament needs to weigh. We do not have the opportunity within this hour, but I certainly anticipate that the committee, in giving a more thorough examination to this question, will afford us that opportunity.
Most of all, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the examination of this issue by the committee will enable all Hon. Members of Parliament, regardless of Party and personal convictions, and will equally enable all Canadians, regardless of their backgrounds, to consider a very important distinction which must be drawn between personal morality and the law; common law or criminal law. We do not need, because of personal convictions, to use the law to enforce those convictions on others. Conversely, we do not need to suggest that in the law being changed we imply a change of moral perspective on the part of individual Members of Parliament or Canada as a society. I do not feel it at all necessary for us to imply any approval of homosexuality because of any change which may be made in the status of homosexuals before the law. Whether we approve or disapprove is a matter of personal conviction which we as individuals take, and have a right to take, and we may insist in taking that stand as individual Members of Parliament with regard not only to our own behaviour but to our own attitude toward other individuals.
All Canadians have a right to equality before the law. All Canadians have a right to what is referred to in the original motion as "human rights". We have those rights for one reason alone, namely, we are people and, therefore, we have the right to claim certain rights and privileges which require no other claim but our humanity.
I look upon this motion in those terms and I welcome the opportunity of this committee and this House to examine this proposal again. But in no way should it imply to the Canadian people that we as a Parliament are changing our attitudes as individual Hon. Members with regard to personal behaviour or
March 26, 1985

personal values. We are but taking a searching look at the rights of Canadians, in particular one group of Canadians, and these are rights which we would want for all people simply because they are people with us.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak very long and I do not intend to address the subject matter of this particular motion. I do however question the necessity to refer this matter specifically to the committee. One reason is that April 17 will be a very momentous and historic day in this country. On that day the equality rights provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms comes into effect. The Government is proposing Bill C-27, which will be discussed tomorrow. The Government also issued a discussion paper entitled Equality Issues in Federal Law. In effect, what the Government has proposed to do in Bill C-27 is to deal with the non-controversial items of equality, which are basically housekeeping matters in the existing legislation, that is, changing husband and wife to "spouse" and changing son and daughter to "child". The Government has then referred the more controversial aspects of Section 15, equality rights, to this special subcommittee headed by the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer).
I personally question the necessity for that particular subcommittee. On April 17 of this year, Section 15 will be the supreme law of this country. No federal majority can in any way change that supreme law because it will be part of the Constitution and of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It will be a matter of interpretation by the courts to determine the extent of this particular section in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Much to my chagrin, and to the chagrin of all those who fought so very hard during the constitutional debate, the Government has not taken definitive action to correct the inequities, imbalances and discrimination which exist in present federal legislation. In that respect, I understand there are over 1,000 pieces of federal legislation. The former Government initiated an audit of the legislation, and it was the intent of the previous Government to amend the laws in major ways to conform to Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Instead of providing the necessary leadership to articulate what the Government feels the definition of equality to be, the Government has decided to allows the whole matter to have more public debate and more consultation. Therefore, the special subcommittee of the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs will travel across the country to hear the views of Canadians.
It was said by one human rights activitist that one does not define minority rights by the views of the majority. It would appear, Mr. Speaker, that that is what the Government is suggesting. The subcommittee will travel across this country and listen to the views of people, and no doubt the majority views will be articulated. There comes a time when the Government has to provide the necessary leadership. There comes a time when the Government has to make the tough decisions. The time has come, in my view, Mr. Speaker, for this Government to tell Canada what it believes to be the definition of
Canadian Human Rights Act
equality, what those words in Section 15(1) mean in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Those 46 words will produce, no doubt, millions upon millions of other words in legal jurisprudence to define that particular subsection.
The Government, by its actions in refusing to provide leadership and amend the legislation to obviate the inequality which exists in federal legislation, is forcing litigation. It is forcing those minority groups, Indians, women, the visible minorities, gays and lesbians and all the others, to fight their battles again. When they fought their battles in 1982, they won and the result was Section 15(1). But now the Government is saying that these people have to refight those battles and come before a committee to articulate again their views and concerns. It will then be up to the subcommittee to make recommendations to the Government. Then they will have to wait, the oppressed and the discriminated against, for further legislation to amend the existing legislation.
It seems to me that if I was discriminated against, I would not bother appearing before this special committee. It would be a colossal waste of time. What I would do is to issue a writ. I would go to court immediately and have the courts define what Section 15(1) means. It is, as I indicated previously, the supreme law of the country now. This Government alone cannot change Section 15(1). Indeed, it requires the consent, as I understand it, of seven provinces with 50 per cent of the population before this section can be changed. I concede that there is an override provision, but it seems to me that it ought not not be used, and I am even somewhat concerned that it exists. Section 15(1) says:
Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.
What is missing is sexual orientation. It is not here. No doubt this matter was debated at length in this House and in committee, and a decision was made. I was not here at the time but many compromises had to be made in order to ensure that we had a Charter of Rights and Freedoms. One of those compromises was that the legislation would be delayed three years in order to allow the federal and provincial Governments to ensure that their respective laws conformed to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, although the previous Government initiated the audit of our legislation and started the process, this Parliament has not completed it. I fully expected that this Government would have introduced that legislation to make April 17 a more historic and momentous day.
The discussion paper the Government tabled, called Equality Issues in Federal Law, indicates that the list under this section is open-ended in the sense that sexual orientation is not excluded because it is not enumerated, but that the items enumerated are not exhaustive. By the wording of that particular section one could challenge discrimination based on sexual orientation in the courts and could very well be successful.

March 26, 1985
Canadian Human Rights Act
I now go back to the process suggested by the Government and the NDP. They are suggesting that this matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, and presumably it will also be referred to the subcommittee which will be travelling across the country. Notwithstanding the fact that I disagree with this travelling road show because I think the Government should provide leadership and amend the legislation and provide Canadians with a definition of equality, no doubt sexual orientation will be one of the items discussed before the committee. Therefore, in conclusion, I question the need for this process. Perhaps the Government is trying to give a message with respect to its position on this Bill. I personally do not think it is necessary specifically to refer the subject matter because no doubt it will be discussed before the committee. But once again, in my view, those who would waste their time by attending this subcommittee would perhaps better serve his or her cause by immediately going to court and getting a judicial interpretation of what equality means in this country now.

Mr. Speaker, as a Member of this House and one who has the honour to be Chairman of the Subcommittee on Equality Rights, I cannot let the comments that were just made pass without some rejoinder. I came into the House this afternoon not intending to speak but simply to be here and listen to what the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) had to say in the course of discussing this Bill, which is now to be referred to the Standing Committee. That is as I think it should be because the subject-matter can then be carefully considered and all points of view can be heard. Therefore, the last thing I wish to do is to talk at length now and run the risk that this Bill will be talked out and the subject-matter not referred to the committee.
But with respect to what the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) has said, I will speak briefly now and when we have debate on Bill C-27 I will return to this Chamber again and speak at greater length, because he has taken a point of view which, if it were to be shared widely, either by Members of this House or by citizens of this country at large, would be harmful to the quest on which we have now embarked to establish true equality among men and women of all backgrounds who make up this country and are proud to call themselves Canadians.
When I hear the Hon. Member say it would be wasteful for people to invest time and energy to appear before our committee, then I think he does a profound disservice to the parliamentary process of this country. When I hear him say that his best advice to anyone would be to issue a writ and appear in court and try to assert his or her remedies under the Charter, then I say that that is the most narrow legalistic view that could possibly prevail. Indeed, I invite the Hon. Member to reconsider the traditions of his Party as well as of other Parties in this House in developing equality in programs and laws as the legal foundation on which men and women can stand and be seen to be equal, not only under the law but before the law.
To say that this is just a matter of law is to miss almost entirely the point and the purpose. The issues that are being referred to the Subcommittee on Equality Rights are not narrow legal issues. Yes, they come from the Constitution. Yes, they involve constitutional law. Yes, lawyers will have points of view on them. But, more profoundly and most important, we are looking at the social, economic and cultural policies of this country which are reflected in laws enacted through the decades. Our quest is to see whether those laws can now be changes. Wherever distinctions are made, we must ensure those distinctions are valid and do not employ any form of discriminatory practice or attitude. In making those changes we are going to carefully consider what has gone before so that we do not take part in unravelling important social relationships that have been developed in the laws and practices of Canada over many decades.
I see, Mr. Speaker, a three part process on which we are embarked. One is the narrow side of housekeeping amendments to eliminate from federal statutes the anomalies that are discriminatory in nature. That is what Bill C-27 is now before this House for. On the other side we also have the process whereby the conflicts and disputes will come before the courts of law and judges will decide whether rights are being infringed upon and what must be changed. That process will indeed start on April 17, but it will continue as long as Canada is a country and as long as we have the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The main purpose and process, the one on which we are now embarked as a committee, is to look at the broad and difficult policy considerations that are thrown up by the new provisions of Section 15.
Put very simply, Mr. Speaker, if we as Members of Parliament do not take that challenge to review profoundly the 1,100 federal laws in order to ensure that they are changed and brought into line with the spirit and the letter of Section 15, then we will have abdicated our role as parliamentarians, and the law makers of the country would be the appointed judges who sit in our courts. I, for one, much prefer to see the laws of this country made in the Parliament of Canada by men and women who are here elected by the people of this country.
I do not shrink away from the consultative process that is embarked upon. I think it is much preferable to have the men and women of Canada speaking on the issues. Reasonable men and women can differ on the issues before us. It is far better that the matter be turned over to a committee to weigh all these points of view and hear them together than that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) should make these points and decide what the laws should be.
The Member for York South-Weston referred with some pride to the fact that the previous Government had started an inventory of federal laws. In fact, less than two hours ago when our committee was meeting we heard from the Minister of Justice that the review of federal laws in light of Section 15 was not commenced within the Department until January of 1984. With that fact on the record and known to other
March 26, 1985

members of his Party, it does not do him any great service to come to the House and lament the fact that there has been foot-dragging on this issue. Along with trade issues, this subject is very much the issue of the decade. It deserves the careful time and attention that it will receive.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but respond to the comments made by the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer). I was indicating that by the Government's lack of action and by its refusing to make the tough decisions, the Government is forcing minority groups to go to court. If one is serious about equality, one would be well advised to go to court rather than wait for the subcommittee to hear deputations and wait for legislation to be introduced in the House. I question what the results of this travelling committee will be. Certain questions are raised in this particular discussion paper. In a news release of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) he asks the question which this subcommittee should address, that is, whether requirements relating to length of employment for maternity benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act should remain greater than requirements for regular benefits.
This issue will be discussed before this special committee and ultimately the Government will have to make a decision. Does the existing legislation constitute inequality? Should the Unemployment Insurance Act be amended? The Government will have to make that decision. It seems to me that the Government wants to govern by plebiscite and public opinion polls. The Government is afraid to make the tough decisions and afraid to protect minority groups. It is afraid to offend anyone. If you are sincere and true and believe in equality, you will make those tough decisions.
By re-opening the old wounds and issuing a discussion paper, the Government is telling these minority groups that everything is up for discussion again. The equality provisions have already been included in Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, but we must now define what equality means. Mr. Speaker, I thought that was what the debate was all about in and before 1982.
Adjournment Debate

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I hesitate to interrupt the Hon. Member, but he did indicate earlier that he had no intention of talking this particular motion out. I would hope that, in the spririt of co-operation which he showed earlier, he might recognize that there is a danger of doing that.

With respect to the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), I did not indicate that I did not intend to talk this Bill out, and I do not intend to talk it out, but I think it is necessary to respond to the comments made by the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore. I have very serious concerns about this committee re-opening discussion on the question of equality. It is forcing these people to litigate if they truly want to further their particular goals. The Government should be making those decisions with respect to the issues that are raised in this discussion paper.
