Mr. Speaker, yesterday, in the absence of the Minister of Agriculture, (Mr. Wise), I put a question to the Acting Minister of Agriculture concerning the Government's plans with regard to meat import quotas, especially as they relate to European Economic Community beef and U.S. beef coming into Canada.
On December 21, after three and one-half months, the Government invoked the meat import law as a result of the massive shipments of subsidized beef into Canada in the fall of 1984. The Government set the quota at 146.5 million pounds of beef. Although it took the Government three and one-half months to make this decision, I think it is a commendable move by the Department, especially in light of representations

March 26, 1985
Adjournment Debate
which we are receiving from the Canadian Cattlemen's Association and other groups.
The quota allotment for the EEC was fixed at 5.9 million pounds, yet since that time the Government has already let some seven million pounds into the country. I understand as well that the Government has negotiated an increase of some 44 million pounds from the 21 million pound quota for the United States, to some 65 million pounds.
According to a CP press report on March 15, it seems that the EEC is demanding a quota of some 23 thousand tonnes, or 51 million pounds of beef. It is trying desperately hard to increase that quota of 5.9 million to some 33 million pounds in this calendar year. They have registered a countervailing duty against a number of farm commodities, such as honey, maple syrup, tobacco, mustard seed and a number of other items, for $51 million. It would appear from the response by the Acting Minister of Agriculture that the Government is proceeding to negotiate with the EEC. However, I see no reason for negotiations when the EEC was dumping subsidized meat in unprecedented amounts by up to 48 cents a pound into the Canadian market in 1984. The historical average from 1978 to 1983 was some 5.9 million pounds and I do not understand why the Government should negotiate for up to 33 million pounds or even higher.
In order to put the question in perspective, the United States allows some 11 million pounds of meat into that country. The United States with 240 million people has a market that is ten times the size of the Canadian market. If that 11 million pounds is suitable for the United States, 5.9 million pounds or less would be suitable for Canada.
The Minister said that he is currently negotiating. I am concerned about allowing the 33 million pounds that the EEC is apparently demanding. This would mean that our meat imports from all sources-from Australia, New Zealand, Nicaragua, the United States and the EEC-would be some 216 million pounds.
It is important for the Government to stiffen its backbone and to stop acting like a jellyfish. It should march into the GATT tribunal in Geneva and fight for our beef producers in light of the 51 million pounds of subsidized beef which was allowed in last year and what the EEC is demanding now. Mark my words, if the Government does not do that, Canada will become a dumping ground for the entire world, because other countries will know that the Government of Canada is not prepared to go to GATT and fight countervailing duties such as the one which is now being proposed by the EEC.
It is very interesting that the Australian Minister of Primary Industry expressed his concern and support for Canada. In fact, I understand Australia offered its support in the GATT tribunal to stop the wholesale dumping of subsidized beef into the Canadian red meat market.
I certainly hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to indicate that the Government is prepared to stand up
and fight for our beef producers and to maintain the integrity of our meat import law which has been set at 146.5 million pounds for this calendar year.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am almost tempted to frame one of the sentences my colleague from Algoma (Mr. Foster) pronounced a few minutes ago, when he referred to a measure taken by this Government as good. It must be the first time. I will have to re-read Hansard, since I have not been exposed to very many words of praise coming from my hon. friend from Algoma.
Mr. Speaker, obviously the Government is not backing down under pressure. However, it is consulting more with the exporting countries, as was announced when the import quotas were imposed. Mr. Speaker, Canada has a number of international trade obligations and rights and as a result, our trading partners are entitled to take part in a consultative process, as is happening at the present time.

In the case of the EEC, its publicly announced intention to retaliate against Canada's system of import controls in accordance with its perceived GATT rights is not the overriding criterion by which the Government is being guided. Rather, it is by our announced intention to work out an arrangement which would continue to safeguard Canadian industry from unfair and damaging import competition.

Mr. Speaker, it is quite clear that a negotiated settlement is preferable to a series of attacks and counter-attacks which benefits nobody and which could not serve as the basis for a long term trade policy. The Canadian people clearly indicated their stand when they elected us on September 4.
I suggest that the era of confrontation is over. We must negotiate and deal openly with our partners. It is all very well to stand up and fight for Canadian farmers. But we are not here to fight but to solve problems. Mr. Speaker, we have solved quite a number of problems since September, without too much fuss about it. What matters is providing Canadian farmers with a sound administration both of our export and domestic markets. That is what the Hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) has been doing all along, and that is what the government will go on doing in the weeks and months to come. There is no need to worry, in my opinion, about the way this matter is being dealt with. I think that we did what we had to do and I can assure the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) that Canadian beef producers can count on our monitoring the situation constantly.
March 26, 1985

subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS-CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS LAY-OFFS. (B) GOVERNMENT POSITION
LABOUR RELATIONS-CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS LAY-OFFS. (B) GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like this afternoon to pursue a couple of concerns I raised in the House about lay-offs at the CNR. 1 expressed concern sometime ago about the lay-off of railway carmen announced in early March, a lay-off which the CNR explained in terms of a reduced workload in the area of passenger rail equipment. This reduced workload is related to a VIA decision not to go ahead with plans to removate old equipment, a decision which I think will prove to be a mistake. When service is restored to several passenger rail routes this June, they will need all the equipment they can get and the new equipment will not yet be on stream.
I expressed concern more recently about even larger lay-offs announced just several days ago of some 474 railroaders across the CNR system. The injustice of this lay-off has been compounded by the fact that the CNR chose to give only two weeks' notice to these workers when normally they would be required to give several weeks' notice. The CNR has used the regulation in the Canada Labour Code which provides that companies can waive the normal notice period if employees will be in receipt of supplementary unemployment benefits.
Yet, many of the younger workers laid off at the Transcona shops, for instance, will not be eligible for such benefits as they will not have worked for the company the required two years, and yet will still only receive the minimum two weeks' notice. In my opinion, this is a violation of both the spirit and the letter of the Canada Labour Code. The CNR should be ashamed of itself. How the president of CNR expects to increase productivity or to improve its corporate image by acting in this way is beyond me. I certainly would not break my back for someone who was ready to cut off my livelihood on two weeks notice in order to improve his quaterly profit margin.
What is needed is a commitment to employment security, something the rail unions are in the process of negotiating. This was in conciliation at the time of the lay-off, and still is. What is the CNR up to? Is it trying to reduce its workforce before it agrees to a no lay-off clause or is it just the usual disgusting tactic of having a lay-off during the negotiation process, a tactic which has gone on for years and years?
I say to the Government and to the Minister that if the new Government is serious about trying to create a new era of labour management relations, it will at the very least instruct the CNR to give full notice to these employees who were laid off as a result of the most recent announcement. If it is really serious, it will order the CNR to cancel the lay-off altogether in view of the fact that negotiations are proceeding at this time, and stop asking railroaders and their families to pay for the short-term financial needs of this Crown corporation.
The CNR has been allowed to rent rolling stock from American railroads. These thousands of cars are not repaired
Adjournment Debate
in Canada, but returned to the U.S. for repair to create and sustain employment in the United States of America. Is this the new Government strategy, I ask, for creating jobs, jobs and more jobs here in Canada? Instead of renting American equipment, we should be employing all the Canadian rail workers we can to repair and maintain our own fleet of rolling stock, both passenger and freight, proceeding with the boxcar rehabilitation program that was planned for Transcona, and eventually building in Transcona the new hopper cars of which a prototype is about to be developed.
Keeping people working on the railroad is an investment in our future. It is a way of increasing the confidence the Government is always talking about. It would be a way of helping put to an end the erosion of the workforce of both the CNR and CPR as a result of short-term profit strategies, combined with an uncritical attitude toward technological change that is increasingly putting employee and public safety at risk.
The work force of the CNR and the CPR has been decreasing literally by the thousands for a number of years. It the railways have their way, it will decrease by a lot more. Whether it be the attempt to run cabooseless trains, the changes at the hump in Symington Yard where far too much is being expected of a new generation computer and human judgment is being removed altogether through the removal of the manual car retarders, the plan to have robot locomotives work in the yard, the attempt to reduce car inspection frequency and quality by utilizing trainmen instead of carmen to do inspections, or the attempt to abolish divisional points like Nakina, Ontario; all add up to a need for the federal Government to yell "halt", and to give Parliamentarians and the public an opportunity to take a second look at just what is going on with the railways in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS-CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS LAY-OFFS. (B) GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to reply to a question asked of me in the House by the then Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie). I know the Hon. Member is aware that some of the questions with which he prefaced his statement will not be answered by the Minister of Labour.
Regarding the plans of Canadian National Railways to lay off 474 workers in Montreal, Winnipeg, Moncton and various other locations across Canada, I would like to explain that under Part III of the Canada Labour Code, 16 weeks' notice and the establishment of a joint planning committee are required whenever 50 or more employees are terminated over a four-week period within a single industrial establishment. The group notice requirement does not alter the fact that each individual employee to be terminated is still entitled to two weeks' notice or two weeks' pay in lieu thereof.
A lay-off does not constitute termination under the Code when, for example, it lasts for less than three months or it is longer than three months and the employee receives supplementary unemployment benefits, or it lasts up to 12 months and the employee maintains recall rights pursuant to a collec-

March 26, 1985
Adjournment Debate
tive bargaining agreement. However, a lay-off is deemed to be a termination whenever the foregoing conditions cease to exist, such as upon the exhaustion of supplementary unemployment benefits, or when the lay-off lasts beyond 12 months in a recall-rights situation under a collective agreement.
A complaint of non-compliance with the group termination provisions in Division V.2 has been investigated by officials in the St. Lawrence region. I am pleased to advise that CN intends to pay each employee five weeks' supplementary unemployment benefits for each year of service, and furthermore that each employee has recall rights for life, under the collective agreement. At this time, there is no apparent violation of the group termination provisions of the Code. The lay-offs in question do not constitute terminations under the Code, because the employees will receive supplementary unemployment benefits.
Regional officials of Labour Canada will monitor the situation in order to ensure that all affected employees receive the benefits to which they are entitled under the Code, and that the provisions of the Code are complied with, particularly since the supplementary unemployment benefits will expire at different times because of the varying years of service of each employee. I believe that that would indicate to the Hon. Member and to the House our intention to ensure that the Canada Labour Code be adhered to. We in Labour Canada are determined always to adhere to the legislation under which we operate.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES-DISMISSAL OF LESBIAN PERSONNEL. (B) REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF NO FURTHER DISMISSALS
CANADIAN ARMED FORCES-DISMISSAL OF LESBIAN PERSONNEL. (B) REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF NO FURTHER DISMISSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 5 last, I questioned the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) with respect to a very serious situation in Nova Scotia in which five women who were members of the Canadian Armed Forces and who happened to be lesbians lost their jobs at Canadian Forces Station Shelburne. At that time, I pointed out to the Minister that the women posed no threat whatsoever to Canada's national security and that they were qualified members of the Armed Forces. I asked him why he allowed a policy to remain on the books which discriminates so blatantly against Canadian gays and lesbians.
1 would like to take this opportunity to amplify that question and express the very serious concern that today in Canada this kind of firing can take place. The current policy of the Canadian Armed Forces is set out in Canadian Forces orders and regulations 19-20. It is a Draconian order. It states:
7. Service policy does not allow homosexual members or members with a sexual abnormality to be retained in the CF.
It goes further. It forces individuals who are members of the Canadian Armed Forces to identify anyone that they may suspect to be a homosexual. Paragraph 2 of the regulations states:
If a person subject to the Code of Service Discipline becomes aware, or suspects that a member of the Canadian Forces... is a homosexual, or has a sexual abnormality, he shall report the matter to the commanding officer-
The military police are then brought in and the individual is apprehended and questioned. In some cases, the person is questioned over a period of days. In this particular instance, one of the women was questioned for several hours in a small room, as if she was a common criminal.
I would suggest that the policy of the Canadian Armed Forces in firing qualified men and women who happen to be gay or lesbian is completely unacceptable. It is a very serious denial of the fundamental rights and freedoms of those individuals.
What is the basis for that policy? In 1981, the former Chief of Staff for the Canadian Armed Forces said that in such a milieu, persons having unusual behaviour traits may attempt to inflict them upon others. He said that there was only one method of assuring the service men and women that their rights would be respected and that was by denying employment to homosexuals. That argument is patently unacceptable. Of course, anyone, anywhere in Canadian society who does not respect the rights of other individuals with whom he or she works is subject to the full sanctions of the law.
Another excuse was given by Admiral Falls. He stated:
As a matter of fact, experience has shown that the presence of homosexuals can be most disruptive. Such disruption often takes the form of physical attacks on the homosexual(s) concerned, and it is possible to prevent this sort of thing only by avoiding the employment of homosexuals in the first place.
We have heard that argument before with respect to blacks, women and other minorities. We would love to be able to employ them but they might be beaten up if we hire them, so we will not hire them! Once again, I suggest that this Parliament should reject that kind of reasoning.
The final argument which was made by the Armed Forces in denying the right of men and women to join the Armed Forces who may be homosexual, and in firing others, is that those individuals may be a threat to national security. There are all sorts of bases upon which an individual might become a threat to national security, but how can it possibly be suggested that someone who makes no secret of their sexual orientation is a threat to national security? Surely, that argument is patently ridiculous. I would suggest that even the Armed Forces today does not attempt with any great degree of conviction to put that argument forward.
Pending a review of this particular policy by the Subcommittee on Equality Rights which has been charged with this responsibility, not only in the context of Section 15 of the Charter or Rights but also in the context of the referral of the Bill which I proposed today that would end discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, I would urge that the Government not wait until that study has been completed. There has been too much pain and suffering inflicted on people who are not criminals, but who happen to be gay or lesbian. Certainly, these are people who are outstanding members of the Armed Forces. I would call upon the Government to institute a moratorium. I ask the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister
March 26, 1985

of National Defence (Mr. Wenman) to give a commitment that, pending the review of this very serious question, and in recognition of the denial of rights of the individuals involved, the Government will undertake that no men or women will be dismissed from the Armed Forces, will lose their jobs and their livelihoods, on the basis of their sexual orientation.
It is not only a source of great pain, considerable financial loss and personal hardship to those individuals who are the victims of discrimination, but I would remind the House that for those many individuals who remain within the Armed Forces, at all levels, and who happen to be gay or lesbian, there is an additional element of oppression by virtue of the fact that they must maintain the secrecye of their sexual orientation. That oppression in many cases is certainly as serious as the oppression suffered by individuals who are kicked out of the Armed Forces.
I have had correspondence and telephone calls from a number of these people, and I emphasize, at all levels of the Armed Forces. Let us bring the Canadian Armed Forces into the twentieth century. Let us recognize the right to equality for men and women in the Armed Forces who happen to be gay or lesbian and put an end to this policy of blatant discrimination.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Wenman (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES-DISMISSAL OF LESBIAN PERSONNEL. (B) REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF NO FURTHER DISMISSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the points and questions raised by the Hon. Member in his question to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) on March 5 are worthy of thoughtful and serious consideration. I am pleased to say that our Government has decided to give the matter that kind of thoughtful and serious consideration through the process of a parliamentary committee. We will follow the work of the committee with considerable interest and await the outcome in the very positive spirit with which the House of Commons has just considered the motion of the Hon. Member.
Referring to the Hon. Member's specific question, as the Hon. Member will recall, the Minister pointed out that he is in
Adjournment Debate
fact part of the formal grievance process which flows from the prevailing National Defence Act. On March 5 the Hon. Member stated, "There is no grievance provision in place for these women". I would, however, like to inform the Hon. Member that several of these former members of the Armed Forces are now in the process of pursuing their redress according to the law. They are now at the level of the Chief of the Defence Staff and could possibly go beyond that to the Minister and, indeed, to the Governor in Council.
The Hon. Member is aware that the Minister made mention of the existing Canadian Armed Forces policy and regulations in this area. However, since the sub-committee on justice and legal affairs has begun its meetings on the broad issues, and since a report is expected from this committee some time next September, it would be inappropriate for the Minister to comment substantively on these regulations and specific cases, so as not to prejudice or disrupt the sub-committee's work.
The Hon. Member is aware that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) appeared this afternoon before the sub-committee dealing with these issues. Parliament will have to await the results of its deliberations and I am sure its report will form an important part of the information for the Government in dealing with these very important issues.
I am confident that the intent and interpretation of the provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms will assure justice and equality among Canadians. The Hon. Member is now assured of his opportunity to express his point of view further in this committee and in this House of Commons, as are those who will present their opinions both for and against these points of view. We look forward to that discussion on behalf of the Canadian Armed Forces.
